steps.instruction: Type this small working example. Run it before adding more.
steps.explain: goto(x, y) chooses a position: x moves left or right; y moves up or down. penup() lets you reposition without a connecting line. pendown() draws the next movement.

steps.title: Replace repetition with a loop
steps.instruction: Replace the repeated movement lines with the loop below. Run and compare.
steps.explain: The for line takes one item from the list at a time. The indented lines run for each item. The loop traces the same points you just wrote separately.
steps.expected: The same practice shape. The code now repeats the movement for you.
steps.question: Which line repeats? Which value changes on each repeat?
steps.answer: The indented drawing lines repeat. The loop variable takes the next value from the list each time.

steps.title: Name the filled shape code
steps.instruction: Replace the tested example with this function and its call. Keep the call at the left edge.
steps.explain: def fill(points, shade) names the code you tested. Its inputs replace the fixed values. The call underneath supplies those values and runs the indented body.
steps.expected: The practice shape should still appear. This step includes both the definition and a call.
steps.question: What would happen if you removed the fill(...) call at the bottom?
steps.answer: The function would be stored, but this example would no longer draw. A definition only runs when it is called.
steps.help: End the def line with a colon. Indent the body four spaces and a nested loop another four spaces. Put the call at the left edge.

steps.question: Which commands actually leave a mark?
steps.answer: Trace the drawing commands. Turns and movements with the pen up prepare the next mark.

steps.title: Test the stopping case
steps.instruction: Add the function and its small test call together. Run before increasing the number of levels.
steps.explain: A recursive function calls itself with a smaller problem. The stopping condition ends the repetition. Start with that case to see the smallest piece.
steps.expected: One smallest piece of the pattern. Compare it with this step’s preview.
steps.question: Which condition stops this function from calling itself again?
steps.answer: Find the if condition near the beginning. The recursive calls move their input toward that stopping condition.
steps.help: Check the changed lines first. Keep parentheses and commas in place. Indent each line inside a loop or function by four spaces.

lines: def tree(x, y, size, angle, depth):
right = (x + ux + vx, y + uy + vy)
fill([(x, y), (x + ux, y + uy), right, top], colors[min(6, 7 - depth)])
tree(top[0], top[1], size / math.sqrt(2), angle + 45, depth - 1)
tree(apex[0], apex[1], size / math.sqrt(2), angle - 45, depth - 1)

steps.title: Add one recursive level
steps.instruction: Change only the test call. Predict how many pieces will appear, then run.
steps.explain: The function reaches its recursive calls once more before reaching the stopping case. Each call makes a smaller copy.
steps.expected: The next level of the pattern. Compare the number and size of pieces.
steps.question: How many smaller calls does one call make?
steps.answer: Count the calls to the function inside its own body. Follow one down to the stopping condition.
